item.title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
item.author: Dara Kerr and Gabrielle Canon
item.content:encoded: A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistanceSebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.Continue reading...

item.title: Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping
item.author: Arwa Mahdawi
item.content:encoded: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and womenYou may be familiar with rule 34 of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.See, for example, Meta’s “pervert glasses”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have filmed themselves trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are harassed by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did not feel the need to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.Continue reading...

item.title: The top five Yankees’ pitching performances of 2026
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: While the 2026 Yankees season has come to a frustratingly early end, it’s hard to blame much of that on the starting pitching. By several measures, the Yankees had one of the best rotations in all of baseball this year, and they have the favorite for the AL Cy Young Award in Cam Schlittler.As part of our season in review, let’s take a look back at some of the rotation’s best efforts of the year. To do that, we’re going to rank them according to the Game Score statistic. Game Score takes a variety of stats from an outing and combines them to try and determine how dominant a pitcher’s outing. Fifty is generally about average, and if a pitcher nears 100, they’re probably putting up an all-time great outing. While we didn’t get any no-hitters or perfect games this year, the Yankees’ rotation still had its fair share of excellent outings, let’s look back at the best of them.This is a post of the top five, but there was a three-way tie for fifth, so it’ll actually include two bonus games too.T5. Cam Schlittler 78 vs. Rays – July 6thOne could hope that Schlittler’s Game 2 start in the ALDS against the Rays harkened back to a regular season outing he had against Tampa Bay. Facing the Rays on July 6th, Schlittler allowed one run on four hits, while striking out eight in eight innings. None of the hits he allowed were more than a single, it’s just that one of them was to the speedy Chandler Simpson, which led to him scoring on another single.Sneaking onto the list as part of that three-way tie for fifth is, surprise, another Schlittler start. This is the only game on the list that the Yankees ended up losing, but you can hardly blame that on the Yankees’ Cy Young candidate. In his seven frames, he held Atlanta to one run on three hits while striking out 11. Thankfully the Yankees scored a run in the eighth and the loss came in extra innings, so Schlittler didn’t get dinged with a loss for that gem.You’ll never be able to guess who the pitcher who had the other game tied for fifth is…While it wasn’t as statistically dominant as his start against the Red Sox in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler’s 2026 outing was still plenty good enough to crack this list. He only went 6.1 innings this time around, but held the Red Sox to just two hits, while striking out 10. The Yankees’ lineup poured it on late on route to a win and an eventual dominant sweep of Boston. If only the rest of the postseason went that well…Someone else has finally made an appearance on the list. Injuries limited Fried to just 112.2 innings this season, but statistically he was still very good. This performance against the Red Sox was part of that. Having been given a 3-0 lead to work with after the top of the first, Fried proceeded to go eight scoreless innings, allowing just three hits and two walks, striking out nine Boston batters.Normal service has resumed as Schlittler matched Fried to tie for third place. However, this was another game where he ended up with a no decision thanks to the offense. In eight innings, Schlittler held the Angels to one run on two hits, striking out nine. The only issue was that one of those hits was a Vaughn Grissom homer that tied the game at one in the seventh inning. The Yankees eventually broke through with five runs in the top of the 10th inning to seal the win, although they deprived their ace of the victory.T1. Cam Schlittler: 84 vs. Phillies – July 24thAs it turned out, there was also a tie for first and, yes, Schlittler was involved. In July, he held a potentially very powerful Phillies’ lineup to no runs in 7.1 innings, surrendering just three hits all game. He struck out 12 batters, including Trea Turner and Bryce Harper twice each.Tying Schlittler for the top spot is a Rodón start that had people wondering what order the playoff rotation should go in. Against the Rays in late September, Rodón threw eight shutout frames, allowing just three hits in arguably his best ever start as a Yankee. He also reached a milestone in getting to the 1500 strikeout mark during the outing.The start — and his stretch run in general — was good enough that it led to people suggesting that Rodón should get the ball for one of the AL Wild Card Series games. In the end, they went with Schlittler, Fried, and Gerrit Cole had their been a Game 3. As it worked out, Rodón didn’t end up pitching at all in the playoffs. You can debate whether that should’ve been the case, but it’s hard to blame any of the starting pitchers for their ALDS losses.Those are the best starts of the year according to Game Score, but which ones were the most memorably good to you?

item.title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
item.author: Dominic Preston
item.content:encoded: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it's a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. item.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
item.author: Lesley Evans Ogden, Knowable Magazine
item.content:encoded: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

item.title: Jos Verstappen was hyped like Max - until it all went wrong
item.author: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded: The degree to which Jos Verstappen’s own Formula 1 disappointment fuelled everything he poured into son Max’s preparation for his ultimately-phenomenal F1 career is already part of motorsport folklore.The element that perhaps gets overlooked now is how good Jos’s own F1 career was supposed to be - that there was a period, a short one admittedly, when there was just as much excitement over Jos’s prospects as a future F1 champion as there was over Max’s arrival on the F1 grid in 2015.As the latest episode of our new F1 Rewind podcast series with Edd Straw and Mark Hughes explores, it’s a test for Footwork at Estoril in late September 1993 that really starts the hype.Only two years out of karting, and having just won the German Formula 3 title, 21-year-old Jos sets a time that would’ve put his very middling car 10th on the grid for the previous weekend’s Portuguese Grand Prix. Track evolution played a part in his time, but the impression his overall performance makes is huge. Verstappen gets the cover slot on the next week’s Autosport magazine, which declares him ‘F1’s hottest new boy’.Edd Straw: “If you look at Jos Verstappen's career record and didn't experience it or live through it, it's really easy to underestimate how big an impact this test really made."Mark Hughes: “He was a seriously hot property at that time. He came straight in from karting and won championship immediately in GM Lotus in the Benelux Championship. He'd done a one-off guest appearance in the bigger league GM Lotus series at Spa. He was sensational in that.“He moved straight to Formula 3, won the German championship, dominated it, and looked set to set the F1 tracks alight.“The teams were falling over themselves trying to get him on a long-term contract. If you were looking for where the next Michael Schumacher or Mika Hakkinen might be, that's where you are looking. No question.”Edd Straw: “Everybody was talking to him basically. McLaren gave him a test at one stage. Obviously Benetton, who he eventually signed for. There was a little bit of Ferrari interest even. It was an absolute clamour because this was the next mega-star.“Also because of how rapid his ascent was. Karting to F1 in two years. In recent years we’ve got a bit more used to really fast ascents, such as Max Verstappen’s. But that was really, really rare at this point.“So you've not only got this driver who is considered to be incredible, but he's on this rocketship to F1 as well.“And if in late 1993 you were saying, ‘right, who is going to come into F1 and win races and be a future world champion?’ Jos Verstappen is the name people would have picked out.”Mark Hughes: “Overwhelmingly at that time. There was no question. He was on the verge of something big.”Verstappen and manager Huub Rothengatter pick Benetton, which is offering a season of testing and preparation in 1994 then a guaranteed race seat - either in its own squad, or placed elsewhere - for 1995.But rather than getting a year of learning outside the spotlight, Verstappen is thrust into Benetton’s second race seat alongside Michael Schumacher when JJ Lehto is injured in a testing crash.Verstappen ultimately gets two stints in that seat, with Lehto still struggling on his return and having to step away again, before being benched at the end of the season so Benetton can evaluate Johnny Herbert in that car. It adds up to 10 of the 16 1994 rounds in the second Benetton, with Verstappen earning two podiums, but also being sent into a terrifying aerial crash on his debut in Brazil in a pile-up triggered by Eddie Irvine and being caught up in the infamous German GP pit fire.Later admitting he found the Schumacher-centric car “too nervous” for him, Verstappen never outqualified or even once led Schumacher at the end of a racing lap in their eight outings together with a massive 1.920s (2.288%) average deficit.Going up against Schumacher in the same team as an underprepared rookie, amid a season of turmoil, was a tall order. And it was enough to instantly crush all that career momentum and hype Verstappen had carried into F1.Mark Hughes: “In hindsight, he wasn't ready, he came in too early. Had the original plan played out, he would have been getting a lot of mileage away from the spotlight of grands prix and would have probably come in much better prepared in 1995.“Not only that, Benetton was absolutely centred around Michael Schumacher and team boss Flavio Briatore was into driver management and then making money on drivers.“Rothengatter and Verstappen had unknowingly surrendered control of his own destiny. As well as being in essentially just the second string car in a team that was totally focused around one driver, Verstappen wasn't even going to be in charge of where he was going to go next.”Edd Straw: “He has this weird season and actually a big chunk of that career momentum's wiped out by that first season. It really, really is. It's not gone. There's still a residual, ‘oh this guy's good’, but already pretty much the die is cast.”Mark Hughes: “It saps you of energy when you get into a situation like that where you're the second driver and you're not the focus of anything. And you've been used to being at the absolute centre of everything. You've been used to being treated as a megastar in the making and with everything centred around you in the junior category, with everybody there for you, everybody on your side. And suddenly to be in the lackey role, I think it does damage you.“And not only that, but you're going up against Michael Schumacher as a rookie.“And in his more reflective later years, Verstappen also said that even disregarding the equipment differences - and there were significant equipment differences at Benetton - and even disregarding all the factors against him, when you looked at some of the things that Michael was able to do close up and suddenly have to say to yourself, ‘I came in thinking I was going to win races, I think I'm going to win the championship, I'm going to beat everybody’ and then you come up against somebody like that and you think, ‘no, maybe I have to recalibrate here’.“And even Verstappen acknowledges that maybe he wasn't Michael Schumacher.“But he was pretty good. Better than he was able to show subsequently.”Watch or listen to F1 Rewind for much more on Jos’s F1 career, including the later big opportunities that fell through, and an in-depth look at how it all fed into the way he handled Max’s upbringing and journey towards F1.

item.title: Searching for a future – The riders still without a contract for 2027
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: The transfer market has been in full swing since August, with dozens of riders changing teams all across the peloton, and dozens more extending with their current teams. Many of these deals are done as early as the spring, with other decisions continuing to be made through the summer.But as the off-season, the winter and the new year rapidly approach, October marks the time when those riders who don’t yet have a contract for next year start to worry. Deals can be struck late on, yes, but rosters are starting to fill up, and with a few big names still on the market, a lot of teams want to leave themselves some flexibility until the last minute.For riders, though, that means they can be left scrambling and having to rethink their futures.At the time of writing, over 120 WorldTour riders don’t have an officially announced contract for 2027, with hundreds more still contractless at the ProTeam level. Some of those may know where they’re going to be racing; it just hasn’t been announced yet, whilst some are still weighing up their options and making a decision, and some are desperately trying to find a spot for 2027.With rosters rapidly filling up, here are some significant names who are still without an official contract for 2027.Various outlets and journalists have linked him with several different teams, including Lotto-Intermarché and Tudor, and there are multiple teams in the peloton that would surely be interested in signing the multiple-time Grand Tour winner and current European TT champion. But so far, the 36-year-old hasn’t been officially tied down to any team, and we don’t know where, if anywhere, his signature will land for 2027.Roglič is in a better position than most, because it seems like he definitely has options on the table – he can certainly continue racing if he wants to – but that doesn’t mean that it’s an easy decision to make. A lot of other deals might be hanging on the outcome of Roglič’s transfer, too, so this is a significant contract to follow at this late point in the window.Former Giro d’Italia winner Tao Geoghegan Hart has never quite been the same since his crash and severe injuries sustained at the Giro in 2023, and though Lidl-Trek put their faith in him with a three-year contract, he hasn’t been able to rediscover his Grand Tour-winning level since then. Now, six years after he took home the maglia rosa, it’s not clear whether we’ll see him in the peloton at all next year.Earlier in the year, the prevailing talk around the paddock was that Geoghegan Hart was set for a quiet retirement, but more recently, Daniel Benson has reported that a move to EF Education-EasyPost could be on the cards.Nothing has been confirmed yet, though, and if a deal hasn’t already been signed, his run of DNFs in the last months won’t have helped in getting something across the line. Geoghegan Hart was once one of the best riders of his generation, but will now likely take a pay cut at the very least, if he does want to continue in the peloton.Lucinda Brand recently confirmed her exit from Lidl-Trek, opting to stay with Baloise Verzekeringen–Het Poetsbureau Lions cyclo-cross but giving an answer about her future on the road. In an Instagram post at the time, she suggested there was news coming on that subject, so it seems likely that she does indeed have a road contract for 2027, but it’s yet to be announced.An extremely experience and successful racer who is clearly still firing on all cylinders, it seems unlikely that Brand would struggle to find a spot for 2027, but the fact that nothing has been announced yet could point to her looking wider than the WorldTour for her future.After nine seasons in the WorldTour, James Knox may be facing the end of the road this season as he has struggled to find a new team, with no extension forthcoming at Picnic PostNL after the expiry of his one-year contract."Of course I wish I did have something," he told at Il Lombardia. "I would still cross my fingers, but the reality of the situation with cycling now, with limited space for the WorldTour teams, many, many quality riders, a lot of focus on points, and younger riders coming through with guaranteed contracts from development teams… I think it's become a situation where it might be hard for me to get anything for next year. I don’t know what will come of it."Though not a prolific winner himself, Knox has established himself as a dependable climbing domestique, but that's perhaps one of most competitive areas on the transfer market, and as a result, it might be a premature end to his road career this winter.Gaia Realini agreed to depart Lidl-Trek this year despite having a year left on her contract, and whilst she reportedly has interest from other teams, nothing is confirmed yet, and we're still waiting to hear the exact details of her future. Often, if riders are leaving teams early, it's because they have a better offer somewhere else already, but it's not always as clear-cut as that. Sometimes things simply aren't working out, or the team want to free up space to bring in another rider by striking a deal with an existing one to leave early, so such an exit doesn't always mean that something else is already lined up.A talented climber with plenty of potential, Realini seems primed to find a new home, but we'll wait to see where.Belgian veteran Tom Van Asbroeck is a mainstay of the professional peloton, and the winner of Classics like Binche-Chimay-Binche as well as a respected Classics road captain, but at 36 he’s joining the legion of older riders who would like to continue their careers, but struggle to find a spot to do so.Van Asbroeck told that he was expecting his contract to be renewed for 2027, but things changed when NSN received "an opportunity the team couldn't pass up" and his future with the team came at the expense of a new signing. "I hope for the team's sake that they have made the right decision, but it leaves me with a bitter feeling," he said. "It is strange that I was deemed good enough for a Tour selection and numerous major races, but now there is suddenly no place for me anymore. That is contradictory and particularly confronting."At the other end of the spectrum from Van Asbroeck, there are riders who are only just starting their careers but find themselves faced with an early hurdle of not having a team. This seems to be the situation facing France's Alexy Faure Prost, who joined Picnic PostNL this year but is facing retirement at only 22."There's only one step between being among the world's best in your category, being courted by the biggest teams, and being forgotten while being even stronger than before," his girlfriend wrote in an Instagram post that Faure Prost collaborated with."Finding another contract back or simply renewing for another year on the same team is becoming more and more impossible. No, ending a professional career at 22 is not normal. Behind all the training data and contract money, there is always a human, not a robot."Will professional sport understand one day that taking young people from junior ranks to the highest level is also about accompanying them? Not just putting them in races. I sincerely hope that a team gets this message and that it's way too early for you to stop showing your talent."Neo-pros must be given a minimum of two years on their first contract, but after that, many face uncertain futures and the harsh reality of the world of future talent, where if you don't prove yourself at a young age, you might not be able to continue at all.As the chances of finding a contract get narrower and narrower, many riders have started to come to terms with the fact that this may be the end of the road for them, and have started sharing their stories on social media. Asbjørn Hellemose did that over the weekend, confirming he won't be continuing with Jayco AlUla next year."With how the transfer market looks at the moment, I will most likely not continue as a WorldTour rider at all," the 27-year-old Dane wrote on Instagram after Lombardia. "At the moment, I’m not sure what’s next for me. When the season is over, I will have time to sit down calmly and reflect on what the best next step for me will be. What I do know is that I’m extremely proud of what I have achieved with my talent and a lot of hard work. Four years in the WorldTour, with participation in one Grand Tour, one World Championships and four Monuments as some of the highlights. Who would have thought that when I was still a teenager living in Denmark?"Hellemose's situation is far from unique, and is a sad one where riders don't get the heartfelt send-off that other retiring (by choice) riders did at races like Il Lombardia and Paris-Tours, but are forced out of the professional peloton when they feel they still have more to give.With well over 100 WorldTour riders still not officially confirmed on teams for 2027, and plenty of squads still with roster spots open for next year, the transfer market is still very much alive, even if it feels like we've seen lots of moves already. There are still plenty more to come, and dozens of riders we could put on our list. Here are a few more:Netcompany Ineos traditionally announce their signings and renewals quite late on, but they have a number of riders out of contract: , and are among themThere are question marks over what's next for , as the Irish sprinter hasn't been confirmed as staying with UAE Team L'Imad, despite being one of the few names to challenge Lorena Wiebes this season. Given her talent, it seems more likely that she's shopping around, rather than struggling for a spot's contract with Decathlon CMA CGM expires this year, and was tight-lipped when asked him about his future at the World ChampionshipsWhilst the lists above highlight riders who may still be trying to nail down a contract at this time of year, there are plenty of riders who don't officially have a contract announced for 2027 yet, but that doesn't mean they're in difficulty. Here's a few of the names on that list and what we know about their futures. will stay with Netcompany Ineos next yearis likely to return to her US racing roots and ride for Virginia's Blue Ridge-TWENTY28has a contract to stay with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Daniel Benson has reportedThat said, there are also plenty of riders without a confirmed spot for 2027 who almost certainly are in the search for survival right now.Human Powered Health and Uno-X Mobility are both full for 2027, with riders like the Pikulik sisters, Kasia Ragusa, Ingvild Gåskjenn and Alberte Greve currently all contractless for next yearThe road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes
item.author: David Smith in Washington
item.content:encoded: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacyDavid Agus’s first encounter with Elizabeth Holmes at a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” Agus, a medical oncologist, recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”Continue reading...

item.title: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold
item.author: Jeffrey Ingold
item.content:encoded: If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …Do you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system.Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and cultureContinue reading...

item.title: Yankees news: The second base conundrum
item.author: Jake Devin
item.content:encoded: The Athletic | Chris Kirschner: The Yankees are reportedly unlikely to give Jazz Chisholm Jr. a qualifying offer, and it seems like the second baseman’s time in the Bronx is just about over. That leaves the question: what do the Yankees do at second base? Captain Aaron Judge seems to have his preferred choice, telling reporters after the Yankees’ ALDS exit, “If we were gonna go win the World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team.” Volpe did look comfortable at second after losing his shortstop job to George Lombard Jr., but Volpe’s work with the bat still leaves plenty to be desired. Luis García Jr. is an interesting option; he’s played second before (albeit with terrible defensive metrics), and looked so skilled defensively at first this year that he could convince you his agility and arm strength would play elsewhere on the diamond. New York Daily News | Peter Sblendorio: There haven’t been many ex-Yankees kicking around postseason, but one former Bomber has figured prominently in Jake Bauers. Bauers played for the club in 2023 and got off to a hot start, hitting a home run in his first game and posting a .899 OPS over his first ten games with the Yankees. Bauers couldn’t keep it going that year (neither could the Yankees) and New York ended up trading him in the offseason to the Brewers in exchange for minor league outfielder Jace Avina, who is now the Yankees’ No. 24 rated prospect by MLB Pipeline. On the other end, Bauers has blossomed with the Brewers, running an .874 OPS this season and taking home deserved 2026 NLCS MVP honors. MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Hoch delivers his offseason preview for the Yankees, running down some of the big questions. Among them is the aforementioned second base situation, as well as the matter of what to do with Giancarlo Stanton, Austin Wells’ future with the Yankees, and David Bednar’s fate. Unlike Chisholm, Bednar appears likely to receive a qualifying offer, which is slated to come in at about $23 million for the 2027 season. The Athletic | Tim Britton: The upcoming MLB free agent class is among the worst in recent memory, and The Athletic looked at the last decade of free agent classes with the benefit of hindsight to get a sense of where this group may fall. The lowest-ranked class ends up as 2017, when the top hitters to sign were Yoenis Cespedes, Dexter Fowler, and Ian Desmond, while the top pitchers were Aroldis Chapman, Kenley Jansen, and Rich Hill. The saving grace for the current crop of free agents is a fairly deep group of pitching targets, headlined by Tarik Skubal but backed up by Michael King, Sonny Gray, Kevin Gausman, and Freddy Peralta. That’s somewhat unfortunate news for the Yankees, who nary need an arm but have an offense that could use reinforcements.

item.title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin wins again on stage 5 as Paul Magnier crashes in final kilometre
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Milan Fretin (Cofidis) struck again at the Tour of Guangxi, the Belgian prevailing in a bunch sprint in Yizhou as overall leader Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) crashed in the final kilometre.As was the case in the previous four stages of the race, stage 5 was always set to come down to a mass sprint finish, and so it proved as the peloton once again raced to finish as one.The sprint was set up after the break of the day – featuring Patrick Gamper, Jasha Sütterlin (JaycoAlUla), Brandon Rivera (Netcompany Ineos), Baptiste Veistroffer (Lotto-Intermarché), Davide Formolo (Movistar), and Max Walker (EF Education-EasyPost) was caught 14km from the finish.Magnier, the winner of stages 1 and 4, looked to be the favourite once again, but the Frenchman didn't make the sprint, crashing along with Max Kanter (XDS-Astana) and several others as the peloton raced towards the finish line.A host of other top sprinters at the race avoided the carnage to contest victory, and it was Arvid de Kleijn (Tudor) who launched the dash for the line. Instead, it was Fretin who came out on top, timing his run just right to beat Matteo Moschetti (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Erlend Blikra (Uno-X Mobility) to the win.Magnier may not have added to his win tally, but he can rest assured that he'll continue in the race lead after the stage, heading into stage 6 with a 10-second lead over stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL), who was also held up in the crash.He's unlikely to hold the jersey all the way to the finish on Sunday, however, with the closing stage heading for the race's only uphill finish at Nongla Scenic Spot (3.2km at 7.3%).The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Houthis Hit Yemen Airport as Saudi Arabia Intercepts Attacks
item.author: Sara Gharaibeh
item.content:encoded: Yemen’s Houthis struck the main airport in the nation’s interim capital on Friday, while its missiles and drones fired toward Saudi Arabia were intercepted, as the flare-up in fighting showed no sign of abating.

item.title: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
item.content:encoded: History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: What one image can't show you about Rwanda F1 track
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: If you adapted the saying 'you should never judge a book by its cover' for the world of Formula 1, then tracks should never be deemed successes or failures based solely on rendered images of them.What can look like nice lines on a bit of paper are no guarantee that a circuit will be good for racing.Equally, corners that are spectacular and a thrill for drivers - such as Eau Rouge at Spa, the Degners at Suzuka, or even La Monumental at the newer Madring - look simple affairs when just viewed on a screen.The disparity between the impression a track render can give and what the reality of a track is like when built is a topic that has come up in recent days following the reveal of the layout of the new F1 track in Rwanda.The single image released of the new Rise Motordrome track near Kigali, which will host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s, drew mixed responses from fans - which was perhaps fuelled by some of the key elements of the layout not being visible.That inevitably prompted debate about whether the track was going to be any good for overtaking.After years working on the project, and thousands of laps of it on a simulator, track designer Alex Wurz is enthusiastic about what has been pulled together.And there are so many details to the circuit, which will feature the greatest elevation change over a lap of the season, that are not possible to pick out from the render, according to Wurz."To give you a little flavour, in Turn 2, we are coming downhill with top speed," he tells The Race. "It's 10.8% [gradient] exactly. We're going into a very high compression with 12% banking, and then going 14% uphill, so you will only see sky."Towards the end of the corner from the 12% banking we are going to 6%, and then 4%. And in the sim, this feels just like pure joy."My favourite section is coming out of the canopy corner over the crest into the lake."The timing of it is that you just get light [as the car rises over the crest] and then suddenly you get a 10% compression, and from there you know your mind has to engage into the fast Esses."Those are the corners I think should resonate with the fans in the simulator, on your computer games, but hopefully with the big dogs - the F1 drivers themselves."An emphasis on 'fighting'As a former F1 driver and Le Mans 24 Hours winner, Wurz knows an awful lot about what makes a top-line track, and what ingredients are needed to help make a good race.He says it is naive to think that overtaking can ever be guaranteed by a track layout because passing is influenced so much by car regulations, details on the day such as tyre degradation levels, and even whether a frontrunner has made a mess of qualifying.What he thinks is critical though is to produce a track that allows drivers to "fight" each other, and that can only come from how corners are sequenced."We have wide open corners with corner sequences 1/2/3, where it means attack, defend, attack, defend," he says. "Now if I defended too much, I might be overtaken, or I'm so slow that the next guy is catching up. So, it is initiating fighting."If it finally is the track where the most overtakes are going to happen, to be honest, that's random. It depends which tyre manufacturer, and what tyre degradation on that day will happen."But it's a drivers' and riders' circuit. It's made for overtaking and fighting, and I think it should tick all those boxes."Wurz has faith that what he has designed will not just be good for fighting, but also be a challenge that drivers enjoy."I think it will be an amazing circuit for racing, but equally for the drivers," he said. "If people like comparisons, I don't like them too much, but with red wine, you speak about berries and oak flavours."So, if we do the same with tracks, you could compare some of the sections to Spa because of the ups and downs and the speed and the flow. Of course, also Suzuka is one of every driver's favourites, and there's some flavours which you could compare."But it's all authentic and bespoke to the topography; it's flowing, it's fast, but we do have, of course, heavy braking areas."One important element that is shared by a lot of tracks is elevation change, something that pretty much all top-ranking venues have.The 197 metres of elevation that the Rwanda layout boasts should deliver something that will make even the straights spectacular, and was not obvious from the render - which The Race has subsequently produced more of.The back straight for example, which was actually hidden from the images, plunges downhill before a proper compression as it rises up again into a heavy braking area.There are also complex braking areas that are being built. "On the render, you don't see the long straight well, and you don't see the hairpins," says Wurz.Effort has gone into creating tight turns with combined braking/turning where drivers are exposed to greater risks of getting things wrong - and therefore being attacked from behind."What is really challenging is if you are combining forces: your braking, your turning, to then optimise all four contact patches at the right slip angle," says Wurz."So those corners where you arrive at 300km/h and you break down to something like 80km/h or 100km/h, but with long combined phases, they are the ones where you can do the real divebombs. And we have three of those."I think those will be the sneaky overtakes. And if you start to defend, again, then your next straight line will be three and a half to four tenths down. And that triggers the fighting."And if there is no overtaking from that, triggering the fighting means someone else is coming. So I think it should at least initiate great fighting."Wurz has consulted a lot of driver friends with ideas for the layout, and says that feedback has been positive.While he has not identified those he has consulted, he says that drivers with a total of 12 FIA world championships have been involved. As chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, the likelihood is that some of those titles were from F1.Wurz thinks that, in order to make a layout a good drivers' circuit, it is critical that drivers have input on what works."I am in almost everyday contact with the greatest champions of current times, so I do show them tracks," he says. "I do listen to what is said about corner sections and which are rewarding and not rewarding."They always have some tips, but the principle layout was seen by one guy who texted me back he said: 'That will be instantly one of the most classic favourite circuits of all drivers.' And I really hope so because it is a lot of work!"And if you want a hint of the way that the track layout has been shaped by thinking about the challenge drivers face, then there is no better example than the Esses section at the end of the lap.Wurz says this area, which looks similar to but is not a carbon copy of the Suzuka Esses, is one that is going to punish greedy drivers who try to attack it too much."If you get one element wrong, the next five or six corners are off," he says. "That's havoc in your brain, but it's joy if you manage it."You are coming around the lake out of the forest corner, which is a really cool corner because it's only forest and the track, and then you come over a hill into a double right-hander."Here the lift in the stomach should be perfectly timed to then get the compression on the apex. And from this moment on, every movement you do on your instruments are important: steering, throttle and brake."None of the corners are flat. Everything has to be either just a downshift or dab on the brake. You really need to flow from one to the next."If you do a little mistake, it's designed that greed is penalising you. And this is so cool for the drivers because you kind of have to hold back a little bit, but you want to exceed it."If you slide half a metre too wide, that means you have already 0.15 seconds gone, so you have to be true to yourself. And this is a type of mind game."Suzuka does it very well. That's why all the drivers love it, and hopefully we can be in the same category of racetrack as the great ones."

item.title: Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
item.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
item.content:encoded: Exclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisisEmployers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
item.author: Aseel Mousa
item.content:encoded: Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marryWijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Austerity is inevitably painful’: How Michael Gove justifies his politics | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast
item.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Michael Gove, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith; the executive producers are Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale
item.content:encoded:
For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on IslamWatch the full episode with Michael Gove here.
Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of BlairFor slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of BooksTo learn more on what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the GuardianPhil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshall a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi BadenochFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper is acute on how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, there’s this paper based on data from the Bank of EnglandFinally, on the Spectator read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in The GuardianContinue reading...

item.title: Evaluating Yankees manager Aaron Boone’s 2026 season
item.author: Dani Mohr
item.content:encoded: Some would say that 2026 was a tumultuous season for the Yankees’ skipper, and there is a lot to be said about what went right in Aaron Boone’s decision-making and what eventually backfired to catalyze disaster.There are many occasions when Boone stepped in at the right time to pull a pitcher and allowed the players to control their own destiny from the plate. He is most confident when he’s defending his guys from the dugout and isn’t afraid to get in an umpire’s face after a bad call. This has always been Boone’s style, and he continued his fiery streak this season with five ejections during regular season games. However, as manager, he is mandated to take accountability for some of the questionable decisions that may have put the Yankees in tougher situations. MLB insiders Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman recently invited Joe Girardi to assess Boone’s decisions, and the former Yankees manager had a lot of positive takeaways despite a disappointing end to this season. Girardi even went on to claim that this was Boone’s best year of managing in his nine years on the job.To give him credit, Boone had to navigate through several injuries this season and consistently found ways to keep the Yankees fighting for a playoff spot when all seemed lost, especially without Aaron Judge. Along with the Yankees captain, several star players had lengthy stints on the injured list, including Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Ryan Weathers, and Giancarlo Stanton. Expected 2026 contributors Cody Bellinger, Austin Wells, Trent Grisham, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. all missed a few weeks, too. Despite all the setbacks, Boone still found a way to propel the Yankees to their third conseuctive season of at least 93 wins, and he could’ve matched the 94 from both 2024 and 2025 had a rainout not nixed Game 162.Contrast this to 2023, when Judge also missed a bunch of time and the Yankees struggled to 82 wins, their worst year in over two decades. Although the personnel may have just been better this time around, Boone did help keep the season from falling apart and rendering September irrelevant (let alone October). Credit Boone and pitching coach Matt Blake for helping the bullpen beat preseason expectations as well; others might not have had the confidence in unheralded names like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, but they had strong seasons setting up for closer David Bednar.The Yankees skipper also deserves some praise for refusing to put Judge in a spot where he could put his future career at risk. After being sidelined for the final stretch of the regular season with a moderate grade right calf strain, Judge was eager to get back into the lineup as the Yankees prepared for the postseason. Boone and general manager Brian Cashman ultimately decided to leave him off the roster for the Wild Card Series against Boston, which didn’t end up being an issue as the Yankees scored a combined 18 runs in the two-game dusting.The Division Series was an entirely different scenario. On the advice of the Yankees’ medical staff, Judge was again absent from the series, in which the first two games were played on the turf at Tropicana Field. Judge, much like the rest of the Yankees’ offense, struggled to put up big numbers in Tampa Bay and went a combined 2-for-10 with a home run, four RBIs, and four strikeouts this season. He appeared disgruntled at Boone’s decision to keep him off the field for the series, but it may have been the best choice to allow him more time to recover from the calf injury and not put his career at risk — after all, severe Achilles injuries have been linked to the soleus muscle, which is where his calf was strained.On the other hand, one of Boone’s most glaringly disappointing choices was putting Grisham in a leadoff spot in an elimination game when the Yankees were at risk of getting swept by the Rays on their own turf. Grisham, who barely saw any action in September, was the last of the batters left to keep the fight alive down 4-3 in the bottom of the ninth. With the hottest hitter of the postseason on deck in Ben Rice—who had been batting leadoff—Grisham ended up striking out in four pitches from Bryan Baker, allowing Tampa Bay to celebrate advancing to the ALCS from the Bronx clubhouse once again. With Grisham putting the cherry on top of an embarrassing postseason performance, the Yankees also continued their postseason losing streak and remain winless on the road since the 2024 ALCS against the Guardians.It looks like Boone is here to stay for at least another year, as his contract runs through the end of 2027. Hopefully the Yankees can make enough clever moves during this expectedly elongated offseason to put them in a better spot for next season.

item.title: The Knicks don’t have to trade anyone to keep James Wiseman and Bruce Brown
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: What I’m about to tell you might blow your mind. Hell, it might’ve blown my mind if I told myself this yesterday.The Knicks are currently facing a roster dilemma. They have 13 players on standard contracts, two below the maximum and one below the minimum.They have two veterans on Exhibit 10 contracts that they want to roster, Bruce Brown and James Wiseman, but they can only roster one and stay beneath the second apron, something that James Dolan has made clear is a hard cap for the team.Brown and Wiseman are different players and represent different things. They rose from a ragtag group of veterans fighting for that 14th roster spot, so much so that the Knicks are doing everything they can to keep both. It’s a dilemma we saw last year with Malcolm Brogdon and Landry Shamet before the former retired to make the decision easy.Wiseman is considered the heavy favorite, to the point where Ian Begley called him a lock. At that point, it would be about trying to find a spot for Brown in a tough environment. To keep both and stay within Dolan’s mandate, they will need to trade someone. The prevailing candidate has been third-year player Pacôme Dadiet, who is buried on the depth chart and running out of time to prove himself as a player. He’s likely on an expiring contract due to his team option almost certainly being declined by the end of October, but his value is still low enough that he’s a negative asset.That has caused the team to shop the more productive reserve point guard Tyler Kolek, but such a move would leave the Knicks much more vulnerable in case of an injury to a lead ballhandler. It’s a tricky dilemma.There are multiple ways that Leon Rose and company can try to sort this out, but there’s one that I recently discovered that would require some extreme savviness and careful day-to-day management.The Knicks can retain both Wiseman and Brown into Opening Night without a trade. It’s risky, but could be worth it.The Knicks have two open roster spots, so just from simple roster management, they are allowed to sign both. Further, they are not hard-capped at the second apron, which allows them to exceed it.The problem, as we all know, is that signing both would push the team over the second apron. While a change of heart is always possible, it would be idiotic and a very bad look if they exceeded it for Brown and not homegrown fan favorite Mitchell Robinson.But what if I told you that the Knicks can temporarily exceed the second apron with extremely little penalty?The punishments that come with the second apron are two-sided. They not only impact your trade flexibility but also harm your future. As a first-apron team, the Knicks are already restricted from doing certain things, but here are the things they cannot do as a second-apron team that they can currently do:Using any portion of the taxpayer mid-level exceptionAggregating two or more player salaries in a trade.Sending out cash as part of a trade.Acquiring a player as part of a sign-and-trade (think why Denver got nobody back for Peyton Watson)Acquiring a player via trade using a traded player exception if that TPE was generated by sending out a player via sign-and-trade.A first-round pick seven years in advance is “frozen” and cannot be used in a transaction. This cannot be undone unless three of the following four seasons are spent beneath the second apron.Looking at these restrictions, most of them apply to the offseason. The only ones that impact the Knicks in-season are aggregating salary in a trade, sending out cash as part of a trade, and, most crucially, the freezing of their 2033 first-round pick.To me, the implications on future draft picks are the biggest reason you don’t want to be in the second apron. If the Knicks exceed it, they won’t be able to use the 2033 pick in a trade for at least four years, something that hurts flexibility as you manage salaries and egos. Not to mention that said pick gets thrown back to No. 30 if you’re in the second apron three times in five years.Where am I going with this? Well, if you read the fine print of the league’s apron policy, you notice one thing in particular.The first-round pick restriction is only if the team finishes a season in the second apron.So, as an example, if a team were to exceed the second apron going into the 2026-27 season, but ducked it via trades at the deadline, they would be exempt from that policy. So for a team that’s perilously close to said apron facing a dilemma… is that worth pursuing?If the Knicks were not to make a single roster move between now and Opening Night, they would go into the 2026-27 season as a second apron team, exactly $1.625 million over the barrier. That would mean they cannot do any of the trade-related stuff up there, but that’s about it.It’s from here that Leon has to work his magic.The simplest way to do this is to bet that you will eventually find a taker for Dadiet or reasonable value for Kolek, allowing you to trade them and shed their salaries off the books. If this happens in one week, two weeks, or three weeks, everything is all good. NBA rules about salary retention state that, no matter when a player is dealt midseason, their full salary is wiped off the books. That means it can happen as late as the trade deadline, and it would be as if they had never played for the Knicks.The problem you run into is that the Knicks lose leverage as time goes on. They don’t have much leverage already, with the league knowing their financials, but imagine a situation in February where they’re trying to find someone to take them out of desperation.To go down this route, the Knicks would have to have confidence that a player could build up midseason trade value, an injury causes a need to open up elsewhere, or current negotiations evolve over weeks and months to make the transaction.The other route would be to keep Brown and Wiseman on non-guaranteed contracts and watch the clock.The two currently each have a cap hit of about $2.45 million, which combined is $4.9 million. That means that the Knicks, with no trade made, would need them to make $3.275 million or less combined to stay below the apron. The exact number that each player is able to make this season on the roster concurrently is $1,636,884.As an example, let’s say Wiseman stays all year. That means he makes $2,449,421, which means that for the Knicks to stay under the second apron (assuming no trades), the max that Brown can make is $812,537. Via the NBA’s prorated salary system, he passes that mark on Black Friday (November 27), so he would need to be cut prior to Thanksgiving to get through waivers.By doing this, the Knicks would use every last penny they have available to them to maximize their roster and give themselves an extra month to figure out what’s going on. The downside here is that you might get stuck in the same spot of figuring out who to keep, plus you would not be able to sign a 15th player in February, which they can do if they cut Wiseman or Brown this week.If all of this cap jargon confused you, here’s a TLDR of the two ways the Knicks can go into the season with Wiseman and Brown and no trades:If the Knicks find a taker for Kolek or Dadiet or any way to cut $1.6 million off their books by the trade deadline, they will finish the season beneath the second apronIf the Knicks release either Brown or Wiseman by November 27 (more like November 25 due to waiver rules), they will save enough money from the non-guaranteed deals to stay just beneath the second apronI find these unlikely, just because it’s a very MyGM way of operating and not one you’d see in a league where you need to balance personal relationships with roster building.But it’s theoretically possible!

item.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permissionIn two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said. “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.” New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday. item.title: Evaluating Brian Cashman’s 2026 season
item.author: Andrés Chávez
item.content:encoded: The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx.A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays exposed many harsh realities that are directly tied to Cashman and his decisions.For the Yankees, 93 wins is not enough. They need to be the best team in the division, because that would bring them additional benefits in postseason play, such as home-field advantage and a ticket straight to the AL Division Series. Everybody in the organization is responsible for how the season plays out, but the spotlight will always point to the head of baseball operations.Offseason moves and decisionsCashman didn’t have a particularly bad offseason, but there were some notable holes when the season started. He didn’t find proper replacements for the rehabbing Anthony Volpe and the underwhelming Ryan McMahon: the former ended up being demoted in early August when the organization promoted George Lombard Jr., and the latter posted a 78 wRC+ and just 0.5 fWAR in 124 games. Volpe eventually returned and played an important role in the stretch run and during the postseason.Extending Trent Grisham a qualifying offer was seen as a moderate risk when it happened, but it was a reasonable one since the outfielder had hit a career-high 34 homers in 2025. The outfielder declined this year, particularly on defense, but at least it wasn’t a long-term commitment.The trade for Ryan Weathers was universally acclaimed, and it was a good piece of business on Cashman’s part. He ended up posting career-bests in ERA (3.60), fWAR (2.5), and innings pitched (137.1). The executive also brought back Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, Amed Rosario, Paul Goldschmidt, and Cody Bellinger.Some of them were nice additions, particularly the 2019 NL MVP, but Cashman left the roster exposed to injuries and underperformance in many spots, and that’s on him, too. The bullpen was a bit thin, as some of his past trade experiments, such as Jake Bird, Ángel Chivilli, and Camilo Doval, just didn’t work. The same can be said about Rule 5 pick Cade Winquest. We are more than willing to give Cashman a pass in the bullpen, since the unit finished with the second-best ERA in MLB, though.Trade Deadline activity (or lack thereof)The Bombers entered the deadline with a few notable needs, which Cashman was very much aware of. They could have used a catcher given Austin Wells’ season-long slump up to that date, a reliever or two, a starter, and a right-handed outfielder.They flirted with several backstops, but ended up empty-handed on that front to the frustration of fans. They did bring in Luis García Jr., who had been enjoying an amazing year in Washington with 23 homers and a 133 wRC+.Heliot Ramos’ arrival was met with mixed reviews, and he posted a disappointing 93 wRC+ in pinstripes. He did have a 184 wRC+ vs. lefties during his time in the Bronx, which was one of the main reasons behind his acquisition. Giving up left-handed pitching prospect Henry Lalane to get him hurt, though. Speaking of…Yes, you could say that the Yankees’ deadline was a disappointment, although some might disagree. However, they managed to keep most of their top prospects, including Lombard, Dax Kilby, Carlos Lagrange, Elmer Rodríguez, and Ben Hess. The promising Lalane was the lone exception.They represent, together with Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Weathers, and Will Warren, the next wave of young talent that will, theoretically at least, keep the team highly competitive for the next 3-7 years. Keeping them all, particularly Lombard when half the league was asking for him in trade conversations, was a win for Cashman.The rest of the farm, however, needs work. A lot of work. The Yankees will need to draft well and be active in the international market in the next couple of years to revamp their depleted system. At least Cashman took a step towards solving the situation, dismissing longtime international scouting director Donny Rowland and replacing him with Mario Garza in January.Player development wins and lossesAs every general manager, Cashman had some player development wins and losses when looking at the final picture of the 2026 campaign. He and his staff managed to turn Blackburn into a very useful reliever with his 1.59 ERA in 85 innings, and he got a nice season from Weathers, too.Schlittler took a step forward into stardom, and Brent Headrick and Warren also improved in 2026. On the other hand, they couldn’t fix Doval, Luis Gil, McMahon, or Volpe, and Jasson Domínguez remains a fringe player. Grisham and Wells were also subpar for their standard.The offense, generally speaking, had a mediocre year with a 101 wRC+ that ranked 14th in MLB. Yes, injuries to Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and other key hitters certainly hurt, but the feeling is that Cashman could have done better, or more.We have said it multiple times in this space: the Yankees need new voices. They need to listen to more prepared people. They can’t keep doing the same things in personnel decisions, player analysis, research and development, and scouting and expect different results. Unless the ownership decides to part ways with their longtime executive, it will be on Cashman to push that change within the organization: does he have that in him, though? It’s at least a fair question.

item.title: US Rep proposes bill to give video game buyers "ownership," not "a license"
item.author: Samuel Axon
item.content:encoded: A new bill proposed by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) aims to establish new regulations that would ensure that "buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," including assurances that they can continue to access the games for years after they are released.The announcement names as an example of the problem the bill aims to solve; that game launched on September 6, 2025, but is scheduled to become unplayable on December 31 due to server shutdowns. The bill, which is called the Power to Players Act, directs the FTC to take action to prevent outcomes like that in the future.

item.title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
item.author: Scharon Harding
item.content:encoded: Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed.This week, some usersreported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.”“I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said.

item.title: Verstappen has troubled qualifying in latest GT outing
item.author: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen and team-mate Chris Lulham and Ben Barnicoat will start only 15th for the GT World Challenge race at Portimao that Verstappen is contesting in his break between Formula 1 races.Verstappen's return to the GT scene got off to an eventful start as he tapped Ezequiel Perez Companc's Audi into a spin in a traffic jam on his first lap in morning practice.Stewards looked at the incident but took no action, and by the end of the second practice session the Verstappen crew was up to fourth.But they struggled in qualifying, their Mercedes visibly running lower than most and kicking up abundant sparks in the twilight session as they managed only 15th on the 61-car grid.While Barnicoat called 15th a "could be worse" situation, he admitted the 2 Seas Motorsport-run Verstappen team had taken a wrong turn with the set-up."We felt like we'd been missing a little bit of speed - we've been quite high up the timesheets but none of us were super happy," he said."So we tried a couple of things there and obviously it didn't quite work out - lots of sparking, a lot of bouncing in a straight line, so I think we just missed it a little bit."The three-hour race starts at 5pm local time on Saturday. The Boutsen VDS Porsche of Dorian Boccalacci, Morris Schuring and Alessio Picariello starts from pole.

item.title: 'Lemon still has juice to squeeze' - Taylor Phinney clocks new personal best for Individual Pursuit at UCI Track World Championships
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Taylor Phinney’s return to competition at this week’s UCI Track World Championships was much heralded, and while neither he or the US Team Pursuit team managed to take home a medal, Phinney was rightly delighted with his performance in the Individual event held on Friday.Phinney retired from the professional peloton prematurely in 2019, aged only 29 after a career in which he won 13 races, including a stage of the Giro d’Italia. But while he is perhaps best known as a road rider, he is no stranger to the track, and though the decision to return to international competition might have been a surprise, that he chose the velodrome as the location for that return was not.Always a powerful rider, he excelled on the track as a younger man, winning the US national Individual Pursuit title aged only 17, before bagging a rainbow jersey winning the same event before his 20th birthday. Back then, he set a time of 4:16.6 - this week in Shanghai he clocked 4:05.529, a massive improvement on his personal best. Although that was only good enough for eighth place, the now 36-year-old was pleased with his ride."Yoooo this one honestly is wild for me to wrap my head around! A PR by nearly 10s in the IP, yes yes positions, technology, etc., but damn, I’m hyped with this one!" he wrote in a post on his Instagram account.While the Shanghai track hasn’t proved to be a particularly fast one, the Individual Pursuit has produced a new World Record, with eventual rainbow jersey, Jonathan Milan, riding a blistering 3:58.850 in qualifying on Friday morning. While that was significantly faster than Phinney’s time, the American’s ride still exceeded expectations."I was hoping to go under 4:10 but once I got out there the vibe was right and the track was ripping. To be top ten with this field is a huge result, something I am super proud of and have worked hard all year for. Felt sooo good to be on my own and tuck up in position and find my rhythm. "When I saw the start list yesterday and they had me tucked between [Filippo] Ganna and Milan in the first heats I’m not gonna lie I felt some weight on my chest. Even before the start, I had no modern reference for going this fast and competing at this level so I figured it could either go alright or I should be braced for the worst. "I held steady at 15.0 laps after starting a bit hot and only started to come undone in the last two laps… I’m so inspired for more and beyond grateful to my mentor Tim Decker for getting me back to this point in just 10 months time."To watch Jonathan Milan rip a world record right after my ride was cherry on top of the experience for me. To see it done, just after feeling it…I want it all baby let’s go! Lemon still has juice to squeeze."At the opposite end of his cycling career, Ashlin Barry provided the US team with its best result in the Individual Pursuit, the 19-year-old finishing in fifth in a time of 4:02.304 and providing a fine follow up to his rainbow jersey in the under 23 Road Race at the UCI Road World Championships.Riding alongside Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson, Barry and Phinney finished seventh in the Team Pursuit earlier in the week, and the country have won only one medal so far, Megan Jastrab finishing third in the women’s Elimination race.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: RFK Jr. proposes FDA look the other way on unproven peptides, report says
item.author: Beth Mole
item.content:encoded: Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Food and Drug Administration is moving forward with plans to ease access to unproven peptide drugs that are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again movement—despite FDA staff scientists finding that the drugs have not been sufficiently studied to establish safety and efficacy and may cause harms.The FDA submitted an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA "enforcement discretion" on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency.The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the FDA, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica.

item.title: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
item.author: Editorial
item.content:encoded: Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbyingJohn Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill.The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing. The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.Continue reading...

item.title: Meta may use sweeping new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees
item.author: Ashley Belanger
item.content:encoded: Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts.Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content.As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans.
