item.title: How Horner, Brown and Wolff made their fortunes from F1
item.author: Darren Cox
item.content:encoded: Christian Horner, Zak Brown and Toto Wolff have been three of the most influential team bosses during Formula 1's extraordinary growth over the past decade.All three have been very well rewarded for it. But the latest set of F1 team accounts filed in the UK reveal something more interesting than simply how much each has made.They show three very different ways of sharing in the value that has been created as F1 teams have gone from businesses that often needed wealthy owners to keep funding them to scarce sporting assets now worth billions.Horner was ultimately a very highly paid employee at Red Bull. Brown has participated in McLaren's growth through a long-term incentive scheme. Wolff owns a significant part of the Mercedes team he runs.The difference between the three helps explain why ownership now appears to be so important to Horner as he considers what he does next.Red Bull Technology's 2025 accounts disclose £66.988million in compensation for loss of office for its highest-paid director, understood to be Horner, alongside £9.029m in remuneration.That puts his disclosed package for the year at around £76m.Some reports have put the compensation above £100m by adding a separate £33.494m figure contained in Red Bull Racing's accounts. But Red Bull Technology explicitly states that its £66.988m disclosure is for the group, which includes Red Bull Racing. The £33.494m should therefore not be added again.Even £76m is an extraordinary sum.But perhaps the most interesting thing about Horner's 20 years at Red Bull isn't what he made. It's what he didn't have: ownership.That should not be confused with Horner having made a bad deal when he joined Red Bull. Quite the opposite.At the end of 2004 he was 31, had built a successful Formula 3000 team in Arden, and was trying to find a way into F1. He had looked at buying Jordan but simply didn't have the hundreds of millions required to make the step independently.Then Dietrich Mateschitz bought Jaguar and turned it into Red Bull Racing.Horner later recalled being summoned to Salzburg and Mateschitz telling him he had big ambitions for the team and was "willing to take a chance" on him. Horner said he was only 31 and "didn't have to think about it for too long".And the deal itself wasn't bad either. Horner has since recalled that Mateschitz told him he wouldn't be paid a huge salary but would receive a healthy bonus for every point Red Bull scored. Jaguar had managed nine points the previous season. Red Bull scored 34 in its first.For a 31-year-old team owner trying to find his way into F1, it was an extraordinary opportunity.Horner helped turn Red Bull Racing from the remains of Jaguar into one of F1's most successful teams, winning six constructors' championships and eight drivers' titles.But however well he was rewarded, Horner remained an employee of a business owned by somebody else.Brown's situation at McLaren is different.McLaren Racing's accounts show its highest-paid director received £81.897m in 2025, comprising £8.215m in remuneration and £73.682m relating to its long-term incentive scheme. Brown has been identified as that director in reporting of the accounts.The bulk of the package resulted from an incentive scheme connected to the enormous increase in the value of McLaren Racing.The turnaround has been remarkable. McLaren was in serious financial trouble during the pandemic and brought outside investment into its racing operation. Five years later, the transaction that consolidated the ownership of McLaren Racing valued the business at around £3.5billion.Brown therefore had a substantial participation in the increase in McLaren Racing's value through his incentive arrangements, allowing him to share in the upside as the business was transformed.The comparison with Horner is striking. Both received packages of around £80m in 2025, but they got there in completely different ways.Horner's was dominated by the compensation he received for leaving the business he had spent two decades building. Brown's was dominated by an incentive designed to give him a share of the value created as McLaren Racing grew.Wolff's position is different again. Mercedes' accounts disclose £9.528m of total directors' remuneration in 2025, although they don't tell us how much of that was Wolff's individually.His executive pay is, in any case, almost incidental to the important number. Because Wolff owns the asset.When INEOS bought into Mercedes' F1 operation, the team was divided equally between Mercedes-Benz, INEOS and Wolff's investment vehicle. Wolff therefore had a one-third economic interest in Mercedes F1 while also serving as its team principal and CEO.That also allows him to participate in the profits distributed by the business. Mercedes paid £125m in dividends in 2025, meaning a one-third shareholder would have an economic interest in roughly £42m of that if the distribution was made pro rata. That money would, of course, flow through the relevant ownership structures rather than simply appearing as part of Wolff's salary.But last year provided a much bigger indication of what his original investment has become worth.Mercedes confirmed the structure but did not disclose the price. The transaction was reported as valuing Mercedes F1 at around $6bn, with Wolff receiving approximately $300m for the stake he sold.And he only sold 15% of his holding.Wolff retained the remaining 85%, equivalent to approximately 28.3% of Mercedes F1. At the same $6bn valuation, that stake would be worth around $1.7bn.That isn't $1.7bn sitting in Wolff's bank account. It is the implied value of a shareholding based on the valuation attached to a minority transaction.But it shows the enormous difference between being paid to create value and owning the value you create.Horner spent more than two decades building Red Bull Racing and was extremely well rewarded as an employee, including a remarkable payment when that relationship ended.Brown helped take McLaren Racing from the edge of a financial crisis to a business valued at around £3.5bn, with an incentive structure that allowed him to participate directly in that increase in value.Wolff did something different. He bought into the business he was running.As the value of F1 teams has exploded, that has proved to be the ultimate deal.Which brings us back to Horner.Since leaving Red Bull, he has become increasingly clear about wanting something different from the next stage of his career.His language now is particularly interesting when compared with the 31-year-old who described the original Red Bull opportunity as a "no-brainer"."I've been a hired hand," Horner said recently. "I did 21 years sitting on the pitwall. I don't need to go back to that."His preference now is to return as "a partner, rather than just a hired hand".It isn't difficult to understand why.The original Red Bull deal was a fantastic one for Horner in 2005. What changed over the following 21 years was F1 itself, and particularly the value of its teams.F1 teams were once sporting operations that routinely consumed their owners' money. Today, the best of them are global sports businesses worth billions.If Horner is going to spend the next decade helping to build another one, you can see why this time he appears determined to own a piece of it.

item.title: Richard Carapaz breaks EF Education-EasyPost contract to sign for NSN
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Richard Carapaz has broken his contract with EF Education-EasyPost early to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal starting in 2027, it was confirmed on Friday.The 33-year-old Ecuadorian was due to remain on the US team until the end of 2027, but will instead ply his trade at the Swiss-registered squad, bringing "world-class climbing ability, experience, and leadership to the team."Announced via a social media video with NSN co-founder and Spanish football icon Andres Iniesta, Carapaz is their seventh confirmed new signing for next season. He raced in the pink of EF for four successful seasons, with the US team posting a video of his recent highlights and behind-the-scenes moments with the caption "Gracias, Richie. Por todo."A former Giro d'Italia winner, Olympic champion, three-time Tour de France stage winner, and winner of multiple Grand Tour King of the Mountains jerseys, Carapaz arrives as a true GC leader for NSN, finishing fourth at the Vuelta a España and eighth overall at the Tour just this past year."For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders," said Carapaz."I’m simply very excited. I’m really looking forward to it, and to be honest, this reminds me a lot of when I signed my first professional contract, when I was incredibly excited about being in the WorldTour. I still have the same motivation as I did that day and that’s really an incredible feeling."I find the NSN project really interesting and after our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the Grand Tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for. "The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together. I think the team has a lot of potential to develop and I’m excited to be part of that in the next three years."Carapaz's total haul of UCI points in 2026 was more than double that of NSN's top -ranked rider, Biniam Girmay, so even into his 30s, he is still among the very best riders in the world and will lead their Grand Tour GC ambitions in the coming three years."Signing Richard Carapaz is a significant moment for our team and an important milestone in the development of our sporting project," said General Manager Kjell Carlström."Richard is a proven champion. His achievements speak for themselves, but what makes him particularly special is his mentality. Richard is known for his grit and determination, and we saw this shine through in 2026 with his two Tour de France stage wins and the polka dot jersey, followed by an impressive podium a week later in San Sebastián."Richard is one of those riders whose passion for cycling is so evident and we believe he still has some of his best performances ahead of him. His experience and leadership will be extremely valuable, not only in helping us achieve our sporting objectives but also in developing the next generation of talent within the team. Richard is someone our young riders can look up to, and I have no doubt he will fit in perfectly in our team culture. We’re excited for Richard’s next chapter at NSN Cycling Team."Carapaz joins Santiago Buitrago, Lennert Van Eetvelt, Kasper Asgreen, Artem Shmidt and Cedric Beullens as new arrivals for 2027 at NSN. He's also the sixth confirmed departure for EF Education-EasyPost at the end of the 2026 season.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Eneco Tour: Mick van Dijke nets maiden pro win as Victor Campenaerts moves into race lead on breathless stage 3
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: After a breathless day of racing, with groups split all over the road, Mick van Dijke (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) took the first professional win of his career from the breakaway on stage 3 of the Eneco Tour in Watersley.The Dutch rider won ahead of new race leader Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike), after the pair bridged across to the original break in the last 33km, before getting away as the lead duo in the last 18km, and battling out the uphill sprint for the win. Jonas Rutsch (Lotto Intermarché) and Pierre Thierry (TotalEnergies) survived from the early break to finish third and fourth, with Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) not far behind and jumping up to second overall as a result of his efforts. Pre-stage race leader Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) tried valiantly to defend the orange jersey, but dropped several times as racing heated up over the undulating Watersley circuit, eventually losing more than a minute and a half and the jersey.Campenaerts now leads overall by 15 seconds from Mouris, with Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) sat third overall on a 30-second deficit. The orange jersey will be decided this weekend over two punchy stages to the Col du VAM and Arnhem."It's the first one. Finally, I'm chasing it already for five and a half years, so I'm super happy," said Van Dijke, then confirming that it was no gift from Campenaerts in the finale, but a result of one rider going for GC and the other the stage win. "I don't know his name, but the French guy [Thierry] was not pulling anymore, and I said to Campy, 'If he doesn't pull, I won't pull'; then he attacked, and I had to go a little bit deep to catch him, but I managed to.""We are big friends; Campy was riding for GC, so I was not allowed to pull. I told him that, and if I helped him a little bit, he did most of the work. Then in the end, he went full, and I also went full."As a tough 110.5km route from Sittard to Watersley welcomed the remaining riders on race day four at the Eneco Tour, a four-rider break found themselves up the road after two laps of the circuit: Rutsch, Thierry, Jesse Kramer (BEAT CC p/b Saxo), and Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam)With 33km to go, four became seven as Hartthijs de Vries (Unibet Rose Rockets), Van Dijke, and Campenaerts attacked across the gap, with the latter's presence – having started the day just 29 seconds down on Söderqvist – forcing Lidl-Trek to chase in the peloton with two reps of the four hills still to come.With 30km to go, Soudal-QuickStep started to accelerate, first with Tim Merlier, who was setting up an attack for Pepijn Reinderink. Quickly, Söderqvist found himself going backwards and struggling, but the riders at the front of the peloton began to mark each other as no one was able to get away. The break started to fracture with the peloton breathing down their necks on the fourth and penultimate time up the Windraak, but the five who remained in front maintained their lead of just under 25 seconds heading into the last lap. As Söderqvist was fully dropped in the last 20km, struggling to hold the wheels, Campenaerts started making his bid for the overall lead in front, taking the maximum six bonus seconds at the Red Bull KM and then attacking with 18km to go from the break. Van Dijke was able to go with the Belgian, making it a leading duo in front of the first chase group containing fourth-place on GC Mouris, 21 seconds back, a second group containing Fisher-Black at 43 seconds back, and the peloton containing Söderqvist back at 1:01 heading into the final 10km. With racing split all over the road, Fisher-Black launched an attack into the last 5.5km, but he was followed by Menno Huising (Visma-Lease a Bike) and the rest of the chasing group he was already in. Soon after, the Kiwi moved across the road and caused Huising – who was looking back at the group – to crash out of the chase. They made no real impression on the leading duo, though; he entered the final kilometre after Campenaerts had done the lion's share of the work. Van Dijke won the uphill sprint for his maiden success, with the rest of the GC hopefuls coming home behind new orange jersey Campenaerts in dribs and drabs. item.title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
item.author: Kate Knibbs, wired.com
item.content:encoded: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.

item.title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.Rather, it’s where 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen shoot out. It’s early in the morning and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes are dense reading, so I am yet to find the section where it explains how and when it’s legal to use such a thing on the road.

item.title: Super Scam Me documentary shows what it takes to catch a romance scammer
item.author: Ashley Belanger
item.content:encoded:
If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account?In a documentary premiering Saturday——investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure. Sneak peek at National Geographic's .
Scamming a romance scammerBroadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year.

item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘New York will explore other deals this weekend and Monday’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: No more fake basketball for the next eight months, folks!The Knicks wrapped up the preseason with their most solid performance, defeated the Raps in New York, and will next see the banner(s) rise to the rafters of MSG.Here’s the latest from everybody and their mothers.On the Knicks’ progress over the past year heading into their title defense:“I’m going to keep it real that there’s something in front of us. I’m not a fan of having an elephant in the room. I’ll address it: It’s about the process. It’s not about the end result. We can’t think about the end result right now. We have a ways to go. This is a new season, new team and we’re gonna have challenges in front of us.“It’s like climbing a mountain. Sometimes you go a 100 yards, but you might get knocked back five yards. Hopefully, it’s not 50 yards, but you might get back five or 10 yards, and you regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way.“But making sure we embrace the process without slippage in that is going to be huge. And if I see us slipping up, it’s my job to let us know as a team that we’re off track. We need to get back on hopefully sooner than later.”On why Jalen Brunson is the NBA’s best leader, as voted by GMs:“He studies the game, and that helps a lot because you can always grow in any field you do. But he walks the talk. He works extremely hard, and he strives for perfection from himself. And when you do that, your peers see you do that, and you’re looked upon as the best player on the team, and it gives you credibility to tell somebody else when they’re not given their all or when they need to do this a little bit better or that a little bit better.”On Brunson’s toughness and willingness to hold teammates accountable:“He’s not afraid because, as a leader, sometimes you can be on an island because you have to always be conscious of ‘I got to do more, I got to do more’ in terms of work harder, focus, everybody’s going to make mistakes, but those little things. And so when you tell your teammates, they can get pissed at you, or they can be like, ‘hey, screw him because who is he to tell me what to do?’ And so you have to have some thick skin because it’s not going to always be you telling somebody to do something, then they embrace it. And I think Jalen has that thick skin and a toughness about him to be in a seat like this.”On Brunson potentially becoming an NBA head coach after his playing career:“I think Jalen has that thick skin and toughness about him to be in a seat like this. You won’t need to, though. My view? If you don’t want to… It’s up to you, Jalen.”On what he expects from the Knicks’ final roster spot:“If one of those guys makes our team, at least right now, they may not even play seven minutes — you know, seven straight minutes. And then at the end of the day, we just have to make a decision.”On the mentality required from the Knicks’ third-string center:“We just hope that there’s a passion and an energy and a focus coming from that spot because, I’m sure at times that person will start, at times they may be the first backup and at times they may be second backup. So as the minutes are fluctuating, you’re going to have to generate some internal energy at times, to go play in a low-minute game.“Sometimes he’ll maybe not play one or two, maybe three games in a row. You look for that, and then you know, you just look for somebody that’s going to play hard at the end of the day – try to do the things that you’re asking on both sides of the floor. And bring a little something different than what the two guys in front of you bring.”On Bruce Brown’s experience, toughness and versatility:“Bruce has been through a lot with a lot of different teams at a pretty high level. His toughness, his experience, his feel, all those things — he’s a winner. It seems like every place he’s gone, he’s won, but all those things can add a lot to the program, and then he’s versatile both ends of the floor. He could play a few different positions offensively; he can guard a few different positions defensively. So a guy like that, especially a veteran winner, can be helpful to any team.”On James Wiseman’s potential and development:“He’s young, he’s talented, you know, he’s raw, still. I think he’s still trying to establish a foothold in this league. But with the God-given attributes he has, in terms of athleticism and length and quickness, [they] can bode well for him on both ends of the floor. And at 25 years old, he hasn’t even reached his prime, especially knowing he hadn’t played a ton of basketball; having a vertical threat at the rim will help [the Knicks], or could help everybody else play the game a little bit easier, whether it’s driving the basketball or playing pick and roll.”On his recovery from wrist surgery:“I had nine different casts. I was able to take it off if I ran or worked out with it. So I had one for workouts, one for showering and obviously one for everyday use.”On maintaining the Knicks’ championship-winning approach entering a new season:“I think what’s most important is that last year we took everything one day at a time. We were talking about — obviously, the topic was getting back to the conference finals and trying to advance. And I think for us now, the way we approached it last year was to take it one day at a time, every single day. So not talking about certain things.“Obviously, we know what it takes, but just going into this with the same mindset for this journey. Even though it’s a new journey, it’s a different journey; the approach has to be the same, if not better.“The first couple of weeks of the season is going to show us who we are and where we are. No matter what we’re doing, whether we’re playing great, playing bad, how are you going to be able to learn? And so, I mean, we’ll find a way. We’ll hold each other accountable, just like we did last year, and then we’ll be better.”On the Knicks’ preseason progress and preparing to defend their championship:“Each game got better and better. Just happy to be back. I feel like it’s a learning experience for us. We have to turn the page on last year and figure out how to get better every single day. It’s gonna be a different journey for us. Our mindset has to be different, and we’ll be ready to go.”On the Knicks’ preseason finale and preparing for opening night:“I thought today was a good dress rehearsal. It was cool, it was very nice to get back out there and get back into our flow and be really good. Obviously we have a lot of things to work on. But it was a good way to end the preseason.”On how he feels physically and his rhythm entering the regular season:“Yeah, I feel good. I feel really, really good.”On who’s the biggest complainer to referees among Knicks:“Josh Hart. Why’d y’all laugh? Did y’all agree with that or something? Everyone behind the camera, I just want y’all to know: y’all just clowned Josh Hart. That’s crazy for y’all to say — in New York, too.”On choosing between winning another NBA championship and a World Series:“Win a World Series, for sure. I already won an NBA championship.”“Before the game starts, I always give everyone at the table, including the fans behind, a chance to really get into the game. Just giving everybody a fist bump down the line of the table, and then go on the court.”On his favorite all-time big man:“I think Hakeem. I feel like, in a way, he kind of is mythical, like Wilt Chamberlain… but I’ve been able to talk and meet Hakeem, and he’s an amazing, amazing human.”On the Knicks’ roster decisions involving Bruce Brown, James Wiseman, Pacome Dadiet and Tyler Kolek:“Brown and James Wiseman have made it through preseason cuts. The Knicks clearly like both players. But New York only has room under the second apron in team salary to keep one player. In order to keep both Brown and Wiseman, the Knicks would need to trade a player on a standard contract without taking back salary. “My read heading into the weekend: Wiseman is a lock to make the roster. There is strong support to add Brown as well. The Knicks would need to make a trade by Monday afternoon if they want to keep Brown. I think they will explore all avenues to make that happen. “It’s logical to assume that the Knicks will move third-year wing Pacome Dadiet. But I believe New York will explore other deals — including trades involving third-year guard Tyler Kolek — this weekend and Monday. “The Knicks will be asking teams to take on a player without sending back salary. To get a deal done, New York may need to attach its own second-round picks (New York will have at least 11 second-round picks in the next seven drafts).”On the Knicks’ handling of Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract negotiations:“So, it was smart to dead the conversation. Now, how you deaded the conversation is the problem. I can’t find out on Twitter if that’s what happened…So if that’s the case (Towns learning from the media that the Knicks paused negotiations), then that’s a communication thing right there. [The Knicks] dropped the ball on that one for one. You don’t let that get outside. So again, I don’t know that. The only thing I’m saying is you don’t break up the family. That’s all I’m going to say. You don’t break up the family.”On fulfilling his childhood dream of becoming a police officer:“It’s something I always wanted to do since I was a kid. I remember back when I was in grade school, elementary school. They asked you on career day, ‘What do you want to be when you grow up?’ And my initial response was a police officer.”On his family’s history in law enforcement:“It runs in the family. My uncle was a captain. His brother was a deputy. My cousin is a captain. My sister’s in the academy. So, it’s a family tradition, basically.”On the physical demands of police academy training compared with the NBA:“Yeah, it was a little bit [more] challenging actually because now I’m running a lot more than I had before. Obviously, in the NBA you run short distances, right? And the police academy, you’re running more long-distance mileage.”On his wife’s initial concerns about his decision to become a police officer:“My wife at first was a little bit concerned because obviously being a police officer, there’s some danger to it. But if you are well-trained and you understand your policies and procedures, you’re able to somewhat have officer safety, which is very important, and that’s the goal.”

item.title: Which mountains will be on the 2027 Tour de France route? Pyrenees back to the fore, one ferociously difficult stage, and other emerging details
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: The 2027 Tour de France looks set to have its major mountain showdown in the Pyrenees next year, with a summit finish on the notoriously difficult Col du Portet a frontrunner to finish off what could well be the toughest single climbing stage of the race.Described back in 2021 by Tadej Pogačar as a "never-ending story," according to La Nouvelle République des Pyrénées, this time round the Col du Portet could be preceded by two historically famous Hors Catégorie ascents, the Tourmalet and Aubisque, making for a ferociously difficult stage.2027's Tour is widely reported to see the Pyrenees taking over from the Alps in 2026 as the scenario for next July's main climbing challenges, with stages 18 and 19 likely the key dates in the country's southernmost mountain range.Other rumours about the major peaks of the 2027 race include an ascent of the Jura's highest paved mountain pass, Le Grand Colombier, as the curtain-raiser to the Tour's climbing stages at the end of the first week. However, as the date of the route publication on Thursday October 22 in Paris looms fast on the horizon, the most striking mountain rumours are the possible inclusion of the Col du Portet. Less famous than the Tourmalet or Aubisque, but also ranked Hors Categorie, the Portet's viciously irregular slopes first appeared in the 2018 Tour. That year it was the finish of one of the Tour's shortest-ever mountain stages - just 65km long - that saw Nairo Quintana take his last ever victory in the race. The Tour then returned to Col du Portet in 2021, when the top favourite both now and then, Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), won the stage ahead of Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) and simultaneously further cemented his considerable overall lead. With Pogačar very likely looking to fight for a record-equalling sixth Tour in 2027, the odds of a repeat battle next summer with the Dane on the same 16.2-kilometre ascent, with many segments at over 9%, are not small. Although the date for the possible ascent of Col du Portet is provisionally said to be stage 18, another day's racing is also expected in the Pyrenees 24 hours later. But in stark contrast to stage 18, no information has yet been leaked regarding potential climbs for stage 19. However, it would seem likely that the stage takes place at the western end of the mountain range, prior to the final weekend's return to Paris.Overall, as reported by , the specialist website in Tour de France pre-route publication news, the first week of the race looks much easier than in 2026. This July saw the Pyrenees feature, albeit briefly, as soon as stage 3, then again in a much fuller format across the Tourmalet to Gavarnie-Gèdre on stage 6.Next summer after the transfer from Cardiff following three stages in Britain and a long hike across northern France, the first summit finish could be on stage 9 at Le Grand Colombier. Another very irregular climb with stretches at 20% in places, the last ascent of the HC climb in the Jura in 2023 saw Vingegaard and Pogačar maintain their stalemate at the top of GC.There were seven stages in the Alps in 2026, and far fewer are expected in 2027, but the few opportunities there will likely be memorable ones all the same. After a rest day in the northern Alps, racing is expected to resume on stage 10 with a visit to the famous World Championships circuit in Sallanches. The circuit's principal challenge, the Côte de Domancy, is both where Hinault took one of the toughest ever Worlds in 1980, and also a preview for the World Championships of 2027, with two highlights being the elite men's road race taking place on the same course next August 28 and the equivalent women's event a week later.Major Alpine finishes are expected on stage 11 and possibly stage 12, with Le Dauphiné Libéré reporting that the first day could see a finish at the Col de Samoëns 1600. Part of the same Grand Massif range which contains the much better-known Col de Joux Plane, the Samoëns climb is a relatively benign 11 kilometres long, and its 900 metres of climbing are relatively steady. The same goes for the next day's predicted big final climb, Col des Saisies, 14.6km or 15.2km long depending on the approach road, but with a gradient never reaching more than 8%. Often used in early parts of the Alpine stages – like in 2023 when the race ended by crossing the much more difficult Col de la Loze – 2027 could be the first ever summit finish on the Saisies. However, its easier slopes once again will ensure the Pyrenees remain the crunch stages of the race.Before the Tour gets there, though, there'll be time for a very difficult stage across the Massif Central, featuring 4,500 metres of vertical climbing, according toand . It is said to finish at the airfield in Mende, which has been the scene of some memorable victories by versatile breakaway specialists like Steve Cummings and Michael Matthews in recent years. But Mende's most memorable day in the GC of the Tour remains 1995 when Laurent Jalabert and the ONCE team all but toppled Miguel Indurain en route to his record-equalling fifth overall win. 32 years later, it remains to be seen if Tadej Pogačar is by then en route to an all-time sixth success, and if anybody is in a position to stop him. item.title: Track World Championships: Great Britain adds two more gold medals on Day 3
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Great Britain continued their successful run on day three of the UCI Track World Championships, taking home more silverware, with Mark Stewart winning the men’s Points Race title and Anna Morris taking the women’s Omnium title in the Shanghai championships.In the other events, Jeffrey Hoogland took a fifth rainbow jersey in the men’s kilometre time trial, while Jonathan Milan backed up the Individual Pursuit world record he set in the semi-finals with a rainbow jersey.With three of the five days complete, Great Britain top the medal table, adding a silver and a bronze medal to their tally, Emma Finucane taking second in the Women’s Sprint and Joseph Truman taking third place behind Hoogland in the Kilo.Great Britain’s Mark Stewart won a brilliantly entertaining Points Race, beating the 2021 rainbow jersey into second place with a powerful and clever ride. Portugal’s Carlos Salgueiro was third.The race finished in dramatic style with Carl-Frederik Bévort only just failing to take a lap, which would have seen the Danish rider take the win. In the end he won the final sprint, but was just off the back of the bunch and took fourth place.Held over 160 laps of the Shanghai track, the 40km race began in restrained style, Red Walters (Grenada) and Ni Li (China) winning the opening sprints, though as the race developed Australian Liam Walsh moved into the lead, taking a lap around a third of the way into the race. However, by the time he reached the back of the bunch, the peloton was in tatters, and he was unable to consolidate, eventually losing that advantage and the 20 points that went with it.Thomas was particularly aggressive, though Stewart was stealthily picking up points behind him, and the pair traded punches all race long, while Salgueiro was closing in. The race swung Stewart’s way with 30 laps to go, the British rider winning five points, while Thomas failed to score. After a first attack from Dévort attack was brought back Salgueiro moved to within four points of Stewart with 20 laps to go and closer still 10 laps later. However, Bévort’s last gasp attempt worked in the Briton’s favour, and he took a career first rainbow jersey.Men's Points Race ResultsMark Stewart (Great Britain)Carlos Salgueiro (Portugal)Carl-Frederik Bévort (Denmark)Moritz Augenstein (Germany)Vincent Hoppezak (Netherlands)Vlas Shichkin (Neutral Athlete)Peter Moore (United States)George Jackson (New Zealand)Fernando Gabriel Nava Romo (Mexico)Dmitriy Noskov (Kazakhstan)Sergey Rostovtsev (Uzbekistan)Anna Morris took Great Britain’s second gold medal of the day, winning the Women’s Omnium, taking her first bunch race rainbow jersey after successes in the Team and Individual Pursuits.Morris rode strongly and intelligently throughout the four race event, finishing the top three of the first three events then defending brilliantly in the fourth. In the end she scored 125 points, beating Tsuyaka Uchino (Japan) and Amalie Dideriksen (Denmark), who was third.Morris moved into the overall lead in event two, the Tempo, while behind her Lotte Kopecky (Belgium) moved up the overall standings, taking second place, with French woman Victoire Berteau in third place.Morris remained attentive throughout the Elimination race, riding aggressively and often on the front, but was the last rider eliminated, with Berteau taking the sprint ahead of recently crowned Elimination World Champion Kopecky.With all the points scored in the Points Race counting towards the total, the final event was hugely important, and Morris started well, taking a maximum five points in the opening sprint with 70 of the 80 laps remaining. Behind her, though, Uchino continued to nag the Brit, riding aggressively, stealing points and closing to within five of Morris at the halfway mark. However, a five woman breakaway took all the points on the next sprint, easing the pressure, and when Uchino was caught behind a split shortly after, Morris's victory was all but secured.Women's item.title: Evans given a hero's homecoming after WRC title triumph
Lawson launches custom guitar ahead of the US GP
item.author: Hannah Atkinson
item.content:encoded: F1 driver by day, musician by… Thursday evening? Liam Lawson will make his debut in VCARB's Garage Sessions music and culture event ahead of the United States Grand Prix at Austin, while launching his very own custom Taylor Guitars LL30 GS Mini Special Edition. The guitar features a pink to white ombre design, and his racing number 30 in the centre.Liam has loved music since his childhood, as his Dad encouraged him and his brother to play from the age of six. Not quite the career path Liam ended up taking, though.The event kicks off on Thursday at Inn Cahoots on Austin’s East 6th Street, with the Esses Bazaar from 3pm, featuring live music, food, western wear, glam stations, tattoos and a chance to get up close and grab a photo with the team’s show car.Garage Sessions follows at 7pm, where Liam will perform live next to his former childhood bandmates, including his brother and two close friends!The wider line up features a mix of emerging talent and established songwriters like Jonathan Capeci, Scoot Teasley, Jess Farren, Alison Nichols, and Drake Milligan.Liam said: “I feel very proud to be launching my partnership with Taylor Guitars at Garage Sessions. Playing the guitar has been a big part of my life since I was young, as my Dad played in a band throughout my childhood. He encouraged my brother and I to play since we were six years old, so it feels like a full circle moment to be launching a custom LL30 GS Mini SE while performing with my brother and two friends who I grew up playing with."Music is a big part of my life, and I use it to clear my head during the season, so I'm really excited to perform at Garage Sessions where we can connect with fans outside of the track. I’m look ing forward to meeting everyone there.”With Garage Sessions bringing together racing, music, and community, Racing Bulls is giving fans another reason to get excited about Austin, and giving Lawson a chance to show off a skill that doesn’t involve a steering wheel.

item.title: Eneco Tour organisers quickly equalise prize money for men and women after Charlotte Kool's Instagram call-out
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Making a major change to the original total prize money of €17,205 for the women's race, and €63,465 for the men's race, TIG Sports & Events have now moved to close the €46,215 pay gap to zero.Kool took to her Instagram to call out the race earlier in the race, saying, "I'm curious if women get a discount at @eneco for energy? Prologue: Same start time, same distance, same energy," after Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) earned €1,490 for his victory on the opening day, while equivalent women's winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) won just €220. "Eneco and Eneco Tour organizer TIG Sports & Events are equalizing the prize money for men and women starting with this edition. The total prize money for women will be increased to the same amount as for the men," read a press release on the race's website."At the formation of the partnership, Eneco and the organisation agreed to operate based on innovation, sustainability, and inclusivity. The combination of a women's and men's race within a single event is an important part of this, as is the equal positioning of the men's and women's races. Both parties would therefore equalise the prize money in the coming years."The race noted how the originally planned prize money figures were determined by "the organisation following the applicable scales of the UCI for the category in which both races fall, and how "These scales have different amounts for men and women." But after Kool's comments, they decided to take action."Charlotte Kool's social media post illustrated that the discussion about prize equality in cycling was even more urgent than we already thought," read the statement. "This has prompted us to accelerate this step. Eneco and the organisation have now jointly decided to raise the prize money for women to the level of the men.""This is top class. I am super happy that it is being picked up like this and implemented immediately," said Kool. "It shows that the Eneco Tour really considers the women just as important as the men.""We organize the women’s and men’s races together and want to give both the same attention. The same performance deserves the same platform," said Race Director Roxane Knetemann. "That is why we already ensure that all teams receive a good expense allowance to start here, which is not common at all races. But that also includes prize money right from the start. It is good that we can realize this together with Eneco for this edition."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
item.author: Nick Indge
item.content:encoded: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn't feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly.Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, "a high performance audience." The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both.The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That's not just consumer purchasing either—that's across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn't been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts.

item.title: UCI cancels Urban Cycling World Championships amid missile strikes on host Saudi Arabia
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The UCI has cancelled the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships with just over two weeks' notice due to the security situation in the host city of Riyadh in Saudi Arabia. Amid a much broader landscape of conflict in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia has come under fire from a series of attacks in recent days that have been linked to the Houthi militia movement in Yemen. In the past 10 days, the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which is where the vast majority of the athletes and staff would have been flying into, has been struck in several separate missile attacks. Both the airport and aircraft have been targeted in the strikes, which have reportedly killed 18 people and injured hundreds more. Several national federations had already taken the steps to withdraw from the Urban Cycling World Championships, which comprises BMX Freestyle and Trials and was set to run from November 3-7. Australia's federation stated on Friday that it "cannot justify exposing our athletes and staff to these risks", citing government-issued travel advice. Several hours later, the UCI and the Saudi Cycling Federation announced that the event "will not proceed" anymore. "The decision follows a joint assessment of recent developments in the region and their impact on the logistical organisation of the Championships," read a statement from the sport's governing body."The UCI regrets having to take this decision and expresses its appreciation to the Saudi Cycling Federation for their support and cooperation throughout preparations for the event. It also thanks the athletes, teams and National Federations for their understanding."The Saudi Cycling Federation reaffirms its commitment to developing cycling in the Kingdom and strengthening its partnership with the UCI. These efforts aim to support the growth of the sport, broaden participation and continue attracting major international cycling events to Saudi Arabia in the years ahead."It is not clear whether the UCI will look to rearrange the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships at some point down the line, or whether it will simply be scrapped for this year. The event was set to have a direct impact on the qualification pathway for the Olympic Games in 2028 for BMX Freestyle. The UCI stated it "will communicate shortly on the sporting consequences of this announcement".The UCI Urban Cycling World Championships were first held in 2017 and took place in Riyadh in 2025 as part of a two-year hosting deal with the Saudi Cycling Federation.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Rocket Report: FAA eyes more Starbase traffic; India's Skyroot snares US customer
item.author: Stephen Clark
item.content:encoded: Welcome to Edition 9.15 of the Rocket Report! The launch I'm most looking forward to in the next few weeks is that of Japan's Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission. MMX is one of the marquee space science missions launching this year, and it's set to leave Earth as soon as Monday (US time) aboard a Japanese H3 rocket. The spacecraft will visit Phobos and Deimos, the two asteroid-like moons of Mars, deploying a rover and collecting specimens for return to Earth in 2031. Exploration at its finest.As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.Reflect Orbital looks to India for launch capacity. California-based Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on-demand with in-space mirrors, announced the purchase of two launches Wednesday from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace, Payload Space reports. One of the launches will use Skyroot's Vikram-1 rocket, which became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit in July. The other will fly on an upgraded rocket called the Vikram-1U.

item.title: Who will win this year’s ultimate F1 dream ticket? You decide…
'Feels like a bowling ball went into my ribs' – Mass pile-up at Track World Championships sees Lorena Wiebes crash out of Omnium title defence – Video
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: A mass pile-up crash at the UCI Track World Championships forced defending rainbow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes (Netherlands) to abandon the Omnium, coming down hard in the first of four events, the Scratch Race, and taking down more than half of the bunch with her. Wiebes was riding towards the front of the pack with four laps to go when she was squeezed in between Lara Gillespie (Ireland) and Elisa Balsamo (Italy), causing her bike to slide out from under her as she lost control of the handlebars and hit the deck at high speed. Riding towards the front, 13 of the 24 competing riders ended up crashing as they funnelled down into a pile at the bottom of the banking.Twenty three riders were able to remount their bikes and finish the race after a restart, with Japan's Tsuyaka Uchino winning the Scratch Race, but Wiebes, who won the title 12 months ago in Santiago, Chile, was a DNF. The Dutch star was left with bandaging on both knees, both arms, and one of her ankles, but confirmed to her home media that she escaped without fractures. "It looks like some handlebars got tangled. From what I can see in the footage, I just held my line. I was focusing on the girls coming from behind and it felt like I was suddenly taken out," said Wiebes to in the Shanghai Velodrome."It does feel like a bowling ball went into my ribs. My knees are pretty scraped and I also have pain in my ribs and shoulder, but I think the damage after this blow is relatively minor."It's the second year running that Wiebes has crashed hard at the Track World Championships, coming down while leading last year's Madison after a botched handover with teammate Lisa van Belle.Already the Scratch Race World Champion in 2026, Wiebes was due to race in the Madison again on Saturday after the Omnium, and didn't rule out a quick return, albeit with some heavy strapping likely needed. "We have to see how things go during the day and if I can do some easy cycling on the roller trainer later," she said, having hobbled off the track gingerly with two Dutch team staff members by her side. "Maybe we'll tape up my body here and there and then we'll see."With three rounds of the Omnium complete at the time of writing, Anna Morris (Great Britain) currently leads the overall standings ahead of the final Points Race.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 'If this is what is felt, we need to listen' – Picnic PostNL's Kemna left 'deeply upset' as he responds to allegations of culture of fear at Dutch WorldTour team
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Kemna was mentioned throughout the extensive investigation conducted by NOS Sport and In De Waaier, published on Thursday and which included interviews with 71 current or former employees at Picnic PostNL, one of them even describing the situation as "a dictatorship." But when he spoke to at the Eneco Tour, he struggled to come to terms with what had been revealed. "The only reaction I can give is that I am deeply upset. That I sympathise with all the people we have apparently traumatised—I don't know what words are being used. I am astonished by it, but it touches me too," he told ."And it also hurts me that we are portrayed this way as a team, and personally Iwan [Spekenbrink, team owner] and I too... We try to lead the team as well as possible, especially regarding safety. "I come from a culture – you know what cycling was like in the old days – that is exactly what we don't want: to have to do something you don't want to do to improve performance. We lead a team in elite sport, openly and honestly. And this is the accusation we receive... I am devastated by it."Kemna was mentioned by name in the Dutch media report by former rider Martijn Tusveld, who detailed how his standing in the team changed when – after being asked for his opinion by Kemna – he openly criticised the team's tactics at the Giro d'Italia in 2020."I became anxious. I thought: I'll keep my mouth shut and say yes and amen. And that's what I did for the rest of the years with this team," he told He said he had emailed Kemna directly last year to tell him he no longer dared to speak up and that he was not the person he once was.Tusveld also said he suffered with symptoms of depression in 2021, stating: "I also thought about harming myself."Kemna responded directly to this exchange, with a different recollection from the rider, and bewilderment after believing Tusveld had wanted to remain on the team even after the Giro incident."I have an email from Martijn Tusveld. I replied to it and invited him, and then things went quiet. Until today," he said. "I feel sorry for him, because I really have the feeling that Martijn is a nice guy; that's how I know him."But what I find a bit hard to understand is that Martijn worked with our team for several years and also clearly indicated that he wanted to stay with our team."'If this is what is felt, we need to listen to it'Tom Dumoulin's former coach, Adriaan Helmantel, also spoke in detail in the report, saying that the management looked to establish more control due to "paranoia" in the wake of their 2017 Giro d'Italia victory: "It became a dictatorship"Asked directly if he recognised himself in the stories, most of which are anonymous, and while noting how his experience isn't how it was described by the former staff members at Picnic PostNL, Kemna did recognise the need to act."Yes, I know those stories, I know the examples too. I also know which sides it touches upon. But that is not the side we are in when it comes to a culture of fear or dictatorship; I can barely bring myself to say it. I do not recognise myself in that at all," said Kemna."If this comes our way and we have no intentions, but if it is received as such, then we cannot simply look away," says the team manager. "We are deeply surprised that this can just happen. We will have to see exactly what it all is, but if that is the case, then we cannot do absolutely nothing."The team reportedly didn't respond when approached by and in person for comment, but did post a statement in response in the hours that followed. They confirmed they would commission an independent investigation into the team culture, and that it would "take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed." Kemna too is looking for clarity."I would like answers, and I actually said that I don't want to stand here to defend everything. I have already indicated that it does affect me," said the head coach."The most important thing is that I find it terrible that people have experienced this. I find that very sad, and the most important thing I must add to that is that we did not acknowledge it, we did not see it. And that we actually can hardly believe it. But it is there. Otherwise, they wouldn't say so."But on the other hand, we also see a lot of people on our team who feel really good. We have been working together for 18 years; we have a lot of different people and very different ways of reacting. If this is what is felt, we need to listen to it. I would like to enter into a dialogue."In response to the developments of the past 24 hours, the Dutch Cycling Union (KNWU) has also released a statement, agreeing with the need for the team's investigation. "The signals emerging in the reporting regarding cycling team Picnic-PostNL are very concerning. The experiences described by riders and staff members affect us and must be taken seriously. The situations described have a major impact on those involved, and they must be able to count on appropriate support," said Wouter Bos, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of the KNWU."Within Picnic-PostNL, a thorough investigation is needed into how this situation could have arisen and what steps are required to prevent a recurrence."As the KNWU, we stand for a cycling sport in which everyone should be able to participate in sports and work freely, enjoyably, and safely. We call upon everyone to report to the hotline in the event of transgressive behaviour, abuse of power, or an unsafe situation. Following this reporting and possible reports, the KNWU is investigating whether, and if so, what further steps are necessary."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The extraordinary figures hinting at Aston Martin's pole potential
item.author: Mark Hughes
item.content:encoded: As the strains on the relationship between Aston Martin and its Formula 1 power unit partner Honda continue and speculation inevitably questions the future of the partnership, it's a good time to look at how the AMR26-Honda is actually performing beyond just the headline depressing Q1 ejections.While Sepang - where both cars made it through to Q2 for the first time - offered a ray of hope, it was dashed one week later in Singapore where Alonso felt certain the power unit's turbo must be broken, so poor was its performance. Honda later reported it could see no failure...It begs the question of just where would this car be if it had a competitive power unit? Is it a mediocre car, a rare Adrian Newey dud, with a poor engine? Or a good car with a truly terrible engine?If we look at the car's performance through the season in the accompanying graph, two things are very clear. 1) The step-change worsening of the car's competitiveness from Barcelona (round seven) to Spa (round 10) as the top teams piled on their developments while the AMR26 remained still in race one spec. 2) The step-change improvement from the car's sole update, in Hungary (round 11). But where does that updated car truly stack up in the quality of its chassis?We can break down the performances further by looking at GPS data from each track and assessing how much time the car loses in those sections of track taken at full throttle (ie mainly the straights). It's an inexact science because of the confounding number of skewing factors* but it does give an order of magnitude picture which is quite clear.The following is quite a reductive stat but a significant one. Comparing Max Verstappen's pole time at Sepang to Fernando Alonso's 12th-fastest time, the Aston Martin driver is 2.090s behind despite having surrendered 2.238s to the Red Bull on the full-throttle parts of the lap. The inference is that with power parity Alonso could've been on pole by a tenth and a half.What is even more eye-opening is that despite the huge disappointment of Singapore, where Alonso went out in Q1 convinced the turbo was broken, the car's corner performance was even more competitive than at Sepang.It's never quite that simple and we'd need to know comparable drag and downforce numbers throughout the compared speed range too, obviously not something the teams are going to release - to each other or to us. But since that Hungary upgrade, Alonso has been driving a car with a balance and poise that he has praised.But the hoped-for follow-up of a power unit improvement from Honda has not manifested. While Alonso's praise of the car on the cooling lap at Zandvoort after getting ninth-place points - "Thanks to everyone at Silverstone. Amazing. A lovely car to drive." - coincided with the introduction of the ADUO 1 Honda upgrade, the feedback from both drivers was that it had lost the driveability gains which had been made with the previous version.When we do the comparison of the Aston Martin to the pole car at each of the tracks since it got its Hungary aero upgrade, we get the following:Laptime deficit when not on full throttle: +1.310s (actual: 2.601s; on full throttle: 1.291s): 1.011s (actual: 2.487s; on full throttle: 1.476s): 0.237s (actual: 3.364s; on full throttle: 3.127s): 1.003s (actual: 3.564s; on full throttle: 2.561s): 2.203s (actual: 4.057s; on full throttle: 1.854s): -0.148s (actual: 2.090s; on full throttle: 2.238s): -0.370s (actual: 2.85s; on full throttle: 3.22s)We can derive a further set of stats from those numbers, that of an implied percentage split of the deficit between power unit-limited and chassis-limited sections of the lap for each of those tracks.: 49.6% / 50.4%: 59.3% / 40.7%: 92.9% / 7.1%: 52% / 48%: 47% / 53%: 101% / -1%: 113% / -13%These numbers suggest the car, even after its Hungary upgrade, was losing time in the corner and the full-throttle sections, but with the power unit forming the dominant part of the deficit, varying wildly according to track layout. But at Sepang and Singapore it was faster through the corners than the pole car.Although factually correct we should treat the above numbers with caution (read the small print*). But they do describe a basic outline, one in which corner performance is more than respectable, recently even very impressive.Worryingly though, as the chassis performance has steadily improved, the power unit appears to be worse with each ADUO upgrade.The ADUO 1 unit came one race after Hungary, at Zandvoort, and the deficit at full throttle increased by a couple of tenths. This may be nothing more than the respective track layouts but, as recalled, the driver feedback suggested little or no overall progress from the power unit there.Attending to those driveability issues via a turbo modification resulted in the ADUO 2 spec, which Alonso first got in Baku. This was the power unit in the car when it had such an encouraging run at Sepang, but the intricate corner-upon-corner layout of Singapore triggered it into a nightmare of terrible throttle response and wildly inconsistent deployment.If the AMR26 could magically be given power unit parity, would it really have been fighting for pole? Not until Sepang, no. Until then, the numbers suggest that since its Hungary upgrade it would have been a high Q2/lower Q3 car. But from Sepang, quite possibly yes. Even in Singapore.But again, there is a disclaimer about that. For it is quite possible that the Honda power unit's unique architecture (with the MGU-K up front, as requested by Newey, centralising the car's mass) has flattered the car's cornering performance. And that with a more powerful, conventionally configured Mercedes or Red Bull power unit, it could possibly lose that cornering advantage.But while taking on board the many cautious disclaimers, we can get an order-of-magnitude idea of the split between chassis and power unit responsible for the big laptime deficit of the Aston Martin. A much more detailed version of that picture will be at the very heart of ongoing discussions between the team and Honda and about what the future might hold for the partnership.*: Some of the deficit of the Aston Martin to pole will be track evolution between whatever session the Aston Martin goes out in compared to Q3. That track evolution will vary from event to event.If we compared the Aston Martin times to the fastest of the session in which Aston Martin was eliminated it would be equally misleading as the quick cars are typically just doing enough to comfortably get through while saving tyres and full power for Q3 while the slow cars are flat-out.The chosen downforce levels will also skew the chassis vs power unit picture (ie low wing would make the power unit look better than it is).

item.title: Eneco Tour Women: Femke Markus solos to victory as Lieke Nooijen defends lead on punchy stage 3
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) soloed to victory on stage 3 of the Eneco Tour Women, attacking multiple times to eventually move away alone 17km from the finish and hold off the chasers all the way to the line.The reduced bunch sprinted out the uphill finale for the minor placings and, more importantly, the bonus seconds on GC, with race leader Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) finishing second to defend her hold on the leader's jersey.Maud Rijnbeek (VolkerWessels) completed the stage podium in third, just ahead of Pfeiffer Georgi (Picnic PostNL). Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) survived the hilly, punchy day to make it to the finale in the main group, but had to settle for sixth on the uphill drag to the line."I’m proud of this victory," Markus said. "We started the stage with a patient approach as a team, but we quickly felt there were opportunities for attacks. So we fully committed to that. "Actually, I didn’t want to go so early at first, but I sensed a moment and thought: I’m taking my chance. But it turned into a long and tough effort, during which I kept thinking: why do I keep doing this to myself? But I do enjoy long attacks and racing like this. To also finish it off is even better."Nooijen now leads the race by 28 seconds over Markus, who started the day 43 seconds down, and will look ahead to the final two stages to try and defend her lead and take home the overall title.Stage 3 featured four laps around Sittard and Watersley, with the Schatsberg climb mid-lap and a kick up to the finish line for a fairly punchy stage. Only 88km long, it wasn't a day where an early break could be allowed to go up the road, so things stayed together for much of the first two laps, before splitting up on a climb towards the end of the second loop, putting stage 1 winner Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) in difficulty.That split came back together again on the third lap, but the aggression didn't let up, with SD Worx-Protime in particular trying to put the pressure on Visma-Lease a Bike with multiple attacks. Nooijen herself had to get involved in the attacks to try to defend and extend her lead, but though the constant digs were wearing down the group, with fewer than 25 riders left with 20km to go, it was hard to make anything stick.Markus, who had already attacked solo earlier in the race, went away again with 17km to go, building a gap of 20 seconds. Visma-Lease a Bike and Picnic PostNL tried to chase her down, but they couldn't reel the strong Dutch rider back in and she soloed to the win. Despite not bringing her back, Visma's work did mean Markus only took five seconds on the line, so Nooijen limited her losses on GC and remains fairly solidly in the lead, after dispatching with Tas who had been at 20 seconds but lost time on stage 3.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal
item.author: Matt Andrews and Ed Walton for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: Landslide blocks river and triggers downstream flooding, while summer temperatures persist in PortugalFlash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged.After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing.Continue reading...

item.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
item.author: Oliver Holmes
item.content:encoded: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearanceA New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.Continue reading...

item.title: Blue Origin is going all in on the New Glenn rocket
item.author: Eric Berger
item.content:encoded: Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities on Friday morning with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there.The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named ). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time.

item.title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
item.author: Ryan Whitwam
item.content:encoded: Android was designed for phones, but that hasn't stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps.Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems.For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that's the problem.

item.title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen

item.content:encoded: As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’ A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.Continue reading...

item.title: Jonathan Milan breaks Individual Pursuit world record at UCI Track World Championships
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The Italian clocked a stunning time of 3:58.850 on Friday, and did so not in a medal ride but in qualifying. That means he still has racing to do, and that he could yet miss out on the World Championship title despite breaking the world record. He could, equally, break his own record later today when he faces Denmark's Frederik Madsen – who also qualified in under four minutes – in Friday's final. Milan broke the world record that he himself set two years ago at the 2024 Track Worlds in Ballerup, Denmark, where he clocked a 3:59.153. He has just taken three tenths of a second out of that. As with Ballerup, the track for the 2026 Worlds in Shanghai is located near enough at sea level, so there wasn't the advantage of the lower air density of a track at altitude, which comes with lower air density. Four world records fell at the European Championships earlier this year, held at a track in Konya, Turkey, at just over 1,000 metres of altitude. Milan's time marks another frontier in the progression of the men's Individual Pursuit world record, which just 10 years ago stood at 4:10.543. The four-minute mark was long seen as a ceiling, but the USA's Ashton Lambie was the first to break through it in 2021 – at altitude at the Aguascalientes velodrome in Mexico – before the Italian star Filippo Ganna nudged it down at the Track Worlds in 2022 in Paris. Great Britain's Josh Charlton took the record for a matter of hours at the 2024 Worlds before it was quickly bettered by Milan, who has now surpassed himself and become the first rider to break 3:59.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
